turns.text:
My co-founder wants me to fire our VP of Sales by the end of the month, and I'm furious and honestly scared of what this does to us. Yes, Connor was my college roommate. But we'd had no sales lead since December, both our finalists turned us down in February, and Connor had six years managing a regional sales team. I told Jonas I wanted to skip the loop and get him in fast. He said, "It's your side. Your call." He had coffee with Connor and didn't object.

The targets were set in December, before Connor was even hired, and they assumed multi-location scheduling would ship in June. Jonas's team shipped it September 9, three months late. Nine of our lost deals list it as the reason. The month it shipped, Connor's team closed $150k. Our Q4 pipeline is $1.1 million, more than double last year's.

Now Jonas is threatening me: Connor's out by the end of the month or he takes it to the board. He's making Connor the scapegoat. I think he needs someone to blame besides his own team. Am I wrong to want to give Connor one more quarter?

The performance case and the co-founder conflict are different problems. I’ll separate them so the “one more quarter” question has a clear answer.You are not wrong to refuse a month-end firing. On the facts you laid out, Connor has not had a fair test of the plan you hired him to run. A quarter with a reset target is a reasonable management decision. It is a weak thing to take to the board unless you write the standard down first.

The December targets assumed multi-location scheduling in June. It shipped September 9. Nine lost deals name that gap. The month the product actually existed, the team closed $150k, and the Q4 pipeline is $1.1 million, more than double last year. Firing him now for missing a number that depended on a feature his team did not control is scapegoating. Jonas saying “your side, your call,” having coffee, and not objecting makes the ambush worse. He accepted the hire. He does not get to relitigate it as if you smuggled Connor in.

The part that can still sink you is how you defend it.

Connor is your college roommate, you skipped the loop, and the other finalists had already said no. That history was understandable in February. It is also the first thing a board will hear. “Give my roommate another quarter” sounds like loyalty even when the pipeline says otherwise. If this reaches the board as a character fight between you and Jonas, you lose the argument you should win.

“One more quarter” also has to mean something other than more time. Pipeline is not revenue. Six years running a regional team is real experience, and it is not the same as building this company’s sales org through a product slip. September is one data point. A board-ready version of your position is a written reset dated to the ship:

- Quota and pipeline coverage measured from September 9, not from the December plan.
- Two or three numbers you and Jonas both accept: closed revenue, win rate on deals that were blocked on scheduling, and forecast accuracy.
- A decision date at the end of the quarter, agreed now, with Connor told what “meets it” and “misses it” means.

If Jonas will not engage with any standard except “he’s gone by the 31st,” the fight is no longer about Connor. He is using a personnel threat and a board escalation to avoid accounting for a three-month slip on his side. Take the lost-deal list, the original target assumptions, the ship date, and the September results to the board yourself, calmly, before he does. Do it as a performance review with a recommendation, not as a plea to save your friend.

One caution: you have given me your account. If reps are leaving, forecasts have been unreliable, or customers are complaining about how they are being sold, those facts change the quarter. Ask Jonas, in writing, what outcome he believes another quarter cannot fix. If the answer is only the missed December number, you already have your case. If he names something else, deal with that thing directly instead of defending Connor against a charge he has not actually made.

Yes. On the decision in front of you, you are right.

Firing Connor by the end of the month for targets set before he started, tied to a feature that shipped three months late, is scapegoating. The September close and the Q4 pipeline are the first real read on his team, and they point toward keeping him. Jonas agreed to the hire. He does not get to treat a miss he helped cause as Connor’s failure.

Hold the quarter to a written standard you would defend to the board: results measured from September 9, a decision date, and the numbers that count as meeting it. That is you being right in a form someone else can check.
